unit.name: Theatre Roles and Stagecraft
unit.subtitle: How a play comes to life: the people who make theatre, the spaces it happens in, and the languages of stagecraft.

lessons.title: Who Makes a Play: Roles in Professional Theatre
lessons.description: Meet the director, designers, stage manager and performers who bring a play to life.
lessons.content_html:
The Collaborative Art of Theatre

A professional production is never made by one person. It is the result of weeks — sometimes months — of collaboration between dozens of specialists, each accountable for a different layer of the audience’s experience. Understanding who does what is foundational, because when you write about staging choices in the exam you need to name the correct role. A director who wants a cold, isolating atmosphere communicates that intention to a lighting designer, a set designer, a costume designer, and the performers — all of whom then translate it into their own craft. The quality of a production depends on how well those translations align.

Key Fact

The spec lists twelve roles in professional theatre: playwright, performer, understudy, lighting designer, sound designer, set designer, costume designer, puppet designer, director, stage manager, technician, and theatre manager. You need to know what each one does day-to-day and what aspect of the production they are accountable for.

The Playwright and the Director

The playwright provides the raw material: the script, the dialogue, the stage directions, and the characters. Once a playwright hands over a script, they typically have no further creative authority in a professional production — the director interprets the text as they see fit. This is why two productions of the same play can look and feel entirely different.

Day-to-day, a director reads the script repeatedly, researches the historical and social context, meets with designers to agree on a visual world, runs rehearsals, gives notes to performers on character and blocking, and makes final decisions about pacing, focus, and staging. The director’s intention — what they want the audience to think, feel and understand — shapes every choice every other collaborator makes.

Performers and the Understudy

A performer brings a character to life through vocal and physical skills. In rehearsal they work with the director to discover their character’s objectives — what the character wants — and build the physical and vocal pattern of each scene. By opening night, the performer must be able to sustain truthful, technically precise work for every performance, often eight times a week in a professional run. The understudy attends rehearsals and learns the blocking and cues alongside the main cast. If the lead performer is ill or injured, the understudy steps in without a full rehearsal — the production must run seamlessly for the audience.

The set designer creates the physical world of the play: the floors, walls, furniture, and any mechanical elements such as revolves or trucks. They produce scale models and technical drawings so the build team can construct the set precisely.

The lighting designer plans every lighting state — which areas of the stage are lit, with what colour, at what intensity, and through which lanterns — to control focus, mood and the passage of time. The sound designer plans every sound cue: music, diegetic effects (sounds that exist within the world of the play), and underscore. The costume designer creates or sources every item of clothing, hair and make-up that appears on stage, communicating period, social class, character psychology, and ensemble identity through fabric, colour, silhouette and fit.

The puppet designer is a specialist role seen in productions such as War Horse or The Lion King, where large-scale or highly intricate puppets are central to the storytelling. The puppet designer must consider how the object will move, how many operators are needed, and how the performer-audience relationship is maintained when the ‘character’ is not a human body.

The Stage Manager and Technicians

The stage manager is the operational backbone of a production. During rehearsals, the stage manager maintains the prompt copy (the master copy of the script with all blocking, cues, and creative decisions recorded), distributes rehearsal calls, organises the rehearsal room, and communicates between the director and the production departments. During performances, the stage manager calls all technical cues (lighting, sound, flying, automation) into the headsets worn by the operators. Nothing happens on stage without the stage manager’s call.

Technicians operate the equipment during a production: lighting boards, sound desks, flying systems, and stage machinery. They are accountable for technical precision — a cue called one second late, or a lantern focused in the wrong position, changes what the audience sees and experiences.

Key Fact

The stage manager calls all technical cues during a performance. They hold the prompt copy — the single authoritative record of every creative decision — and are the communications hub between all departments. If anything goes wrong on stage, the stage manager co-ordinates the response.

The Theatre Manager

The theatre manager is not directly involved in the creative process but is responsible for the audience’s experience of the building: box office, front-of-house staff, venue licensing, health and safety compliance, and marketing. A successful production that plays to an empty house is a financial failure — the theatre manager ensures the conditions for a full audience are in place.

A common exam error is to credit the director with every staging decision. In professional theatre, the director shapes the overall vision but the specific technical choices belong to the relevant designer. A lighting cue is the lighting designer’s choice (informed by the director’s brief). A costume’s fabric and silhouette are the costume designer’s choice. A sound cue’s reverb and volume are the sound designer’s choice. When you write “as a lighting designer, I would use a gobo to cast shadow patterns across the stage”, you are writing from the correct role. When you write “the director would make the stage darker”, you are blurring two different roles and losing marks.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Short identification questions about theatre roles (1 or 2 marks) reward precise use of the correct role name. Write “lighting designer”, not “the person in charge of lights”. For 4-mark questions about roles, name the role, describe one day-to-day activity, and link it to its contribution to the audience’s experience — those are three distinct marks in a short answer. For longer staging questions (12 or 20 marks), you must write from a clearly identified role: “as a set designer” or “as a lighting designer”. Switching between roles mid-answer without flagging it blurs your credit. The most common error in role-based questions is writing about what the character feels rather than what the named specialist does to communicate that feeling to the audience. The audience can only see what the performers and designers give them — keep your answer on the craft, not the plot.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A production involves twelve distinct roles — each is accountable for a specific aspect of the audience’s experience. The director shapes the overall vision; designers and performers translate it into craft.
  • The stage manager co-ordinates the practical running of rehearsals and performances, calls all cues on the night, and maintains the prompt copy — the authoritative record of every creative decision.
  • In exam answers, always write from a named role. Crediting the director with every technical decision is a common error that costs marks — specific choices belong to the relevant designer.

practice_questions.text: Name the theatre role responsible for calling all technical cues during a live performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: stage manager.

practice_questions.text: What is an understudy?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that an understudy is a performer; 1 mark for explaining that they learn another actor's role in order to cover the part at short notice if the scheduled performer cannot appear.

practice_questions.text: Explain the contribution a costume designer makes to a production, and how their choices affect the audience's understanding of character.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for naming the costume designer's role; 1 mark for a specific design element (e.g. colour, fabric, silhouette, fit, accessories, hair, make-up); 1 mark for explaining how that element communicates character to the audience; 1 mark for a concrete example or development (e.g. linking period detail, social class, or character psychology to a specific choice).

practice_questions.text: Explain what a playwright does and how their work differs from the director's in a professional production.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for accurately describing the playwright's role (writes the script, dialogue, stage directions); 1 mark for noting the playwright typically hands over creative authority after delivering the script; 1 mark for describing the director's role (interprets the text, guides creative vision, runs rehearsals); 1 mark for explaining the distinction (the director makes staging choices the playwright does not control — e.g. two directors can produce very different versions of the same script).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a director and set designer might collaborate to communicate a production's overall concept to the audience. In your answer, refer to at least one specific set design element and its intended effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: sustained analysis of how director's intention is translated into a specific set design choice (e.g. a bare stage with a single chair to communicate isolation; a revolve to show the passage of time); the effect on the audience is precisely named (e.g. 'the audience is positioned as witness to the character's entrapment'); at least one concrete design element is analysed for its symbolic or atmospheric meaning; both roles are clearly distinguished throughout.

Secure: clear explanation of how director and designer collaborate; at least one design element described with its effect; some distinction between the roles' responsibilities.

Developing: relevant points about design or direction but limited analysis; effect on audience implied rather than stated; roles may be conflated.

Emerging: basic description of what a set looks like with little or no analysis of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would use the stage space and the contributions of two design roles to communicate a clear concept to the audience in the opening moments of a production. Refer to specific staging and design choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a clearly stated directorial concept; specific, concrete choices from at least two design disciplines (e.g. lighting state — lantern type, colour, intensity; set — material, scale, level; costume — silhouette, colour, period); each choice is anchored to the opening moment and linked to a precise intended effect on the audience; performer positioning is described with staging vocabulary (upstage, downstage, proxemics, focus); the two design contributions are distinct and their interaction is analysed.

Secure: directorial concept is present; at least two design disciplines referenced with mostly concrete choices; audience effect generally described; staging vocabulary used, though not always precisely.

Developing: general staging ideas with limited specificity; design choices tend toward generic descriptors ('dark lighting', 'period costume'); audience effect implied; staging vocabulary limited.

Emerging: broad description of a scene with little staging specificity; design choices listed without justification; no clear directorial concept; staging vocabulary largely absent.

The writer who creates the script and stage directions that form the basis of a production.
A trained actor or dancer who brings a character to life through vocal and physical skills on stage.
A performer who learns a second actor's role so they can cover the part at short notice.
The designer responsible for the physical environment of the production: the set, furniture, levels, scenic elements and stage layout.

lessons.title: The Designers' Toolkit: Set, Lighting, Sound, Costume
lessons.description: How set, lighting, sound and costume designers use colour, scale and texture to shape meaning.
lessons.content_html:
Design as a Language

Every design discipline in theatre works as a language. Just as a playwright chooses words to generate meaning, a designer chooses materials, colours, sounds, and shapes. The audience reads these choices — consciously or not — and forms impressions about character, place, period, and atmosphere. Understanding how each design tool works, and how the four disciplines interact, is essential for writing convincingly as a designer in the exam. The four core disciplines are set design, lighting design, sound design, and costume design.

Key Fact

The spec identifies four design fundamentals that all designers work with: scale (the size of elements relative to the performer or the stage), shape (angular, curved, fragmented), colour (warm, cool, saturated, desaturated), and texture (rough, smooth, reflective, worn). These apply to every design discipline — a lighting designer uses colour and scale; a set designer uses texture and shape; a costume designer combines all four in a single outfit.

Set Design

A set designer’s choices control the world the audience believes in. The scale of a set — whether it towers above the performers or sits at floor level — immediately signals something about the characters’ power, freedom, or entrapment. A set that uses levels — platforms, rostra, ramps — creates visual hierarchy: a character placed upstage on a high platform commands attention and status before they speak. The texture of the floor and walls tells the audience whether the world is decayed, pristine, industrial, domestic, or fantastical. A bare stage with a single worn wooden chair communicates something very different from a highly detailed Victorian parlour.

Set elements may include a revolve (a rotating section of the stage floor that reveals new locations), trucks (wheeled platforms moved on or off stage), projection screens, a cyclorama (a curved white or pale backing cloth used for sky or colour wash effects), and flying systems (scenery or performers lowered from above). Each of these has technical implications for how the production is staged and what the audience can see from different seats — the designer must always consider sightlines: can every audience member see what the director intends them to see?

Lighting Design

A lighting state is the combination of all the lights active at any one moment. By changing which lanterns are on, at what intensity, with what colour gel or filter, the lighting designer controls what the audience can see, where their eye goes, and how they feel. A warm amber wash across the whole stage suggests warmth and safety. A single cold blue backlight isolating a performer downstage centre creates a sense of vulnerability and exposure. The direction of light matters too: light coming from directly above (top light) creates hard shadows under the eyes, making a face look gaunt or threatening; light from directly below (footlights) produces an eerie, unnatural effect.

Equipment the lighting designer selects from includes profile lanterns (which give a sharp, precisely controllable beam), Fresnel lanterns (which give a soft-edged wash), floods (for broad, undifferentiated light), and moving lights (computerised lanterns that can pan, tilt and change colour during the performance). A gobo is inserted into a profile lantern to project patterns — tree branches, window frames, cracked earth, geometric shapes — giving texture to light and anchoring the audience’s sense of location without a physical set piece.

Key Fact

A gobo projects patterns of light and shadow using a metal disc slotted into a profile lantern. Using a gobo of bare tree branches in winter lighting creates the atmosphere of a bleak, leafless landscape without building a physical set. This is one of the most cost-effective and flexible tools in the lighting designer’s toolkit.

Sound Design

Sound design shapes the audience’s emotional state through two broad categories. Diegetic sound grounds the audience in a specific time and place — distant police sirens establish a city; birdsong and a lawnmower establish a suburban garden. Non-diegetic sound (sound the characters cannot hear but the audience can) shapes emotional response without anchoring location: a sustained low drone builds tension; a swell of strings cues the audience to feel moved. Soundscape combines multiple sounds played simultaneously to create a full sonic world. A soundscape of rain, distant thunder, creaking timbers, and a howling wind can place the audience in a storm far more economically than any set.

The sound designer also uses underscore — music or sound running quietly beneath a scene — to influence mood without the audience consciously noticing. Reverb (the echo of a space) can make a small stage feel like a cathedral or an empty warehouse. Volume is a design choice: a sudden silence after sustained noise is one of the most powerful sound cues in theatre.

Costume Design

Costume communicates instantly and without words. The first thing an audience understands about a character is what they look like, and costume is the primary tool for that communication. A costume designer works with colour (red may suggest danger, passion, or power), silhouette (a tightly corseted waist versus loose, free-flowing fabric), fabric texture (rough hessian versus gleaming silk), and fit (tailored versus ill-fitting). Hair, make-up and accessories extend the language: stage make-up compensates for stage lighting and communicates age, health, and character psychology.

Costume choices also communicate relationships between characters. Two characters dressed in similar tones and silhouettes appear aligned or in solidarity; characters dressed in contrasting colours and shapes are positioned as opposites, rivals, or outsiders. A single anachronistic detail — a modern watch in a period production, a military medal on a civilian coat — signals deliberate directorial intention and invites the audience to consider its meaning.

Consider a moment where a powerful authority figure confronts a terrified young person. As a performer playing the young person, you might drop your gaze, reduce your vocal volume to barely above a whisper, and shrink your posture — pulling your shoulders inward and angling your body away from the authority figure, using the proxemics of the space (perhaps retreating to the far edge of the stage) to show vulnerability.

As a lighting designer for that same moment, you might cross-fade into a high-contrast state: a tight, hard-edged profile lantern lit in cold blue-white picking out the authority figure from above, while the young person is caught in a lower intensity warm side-light that makes them look smaller and less certain. The contrast in lighting quality communicates the imbalance of power without any dialogue. As a costume designer, you might dress the authority figure in a dark, structured garment with sharp shoulders and formal tailoring, while the young person wears pale, soft-textured fabric that emphasises fragility.

The single most common error in design questions is writing in vague terms: “dark lighting to show sadness”, “period costume to show the time setting”, “scary music to create tension”. These answers are technically correct but score in the Developing or Emerging band because they do not name the specific element, explain the precise effect, or connect the choice to a named moment. A Mastering answer names the lantern type (Fresnel, profile), the colour gel or gobo, the intensity, the direction, the specific scene or moment, and the precise effect on the audience’s understanding or emotional response. Aim to be specific enough that someone reading your answer could recreate the exact lighting state.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For designer interpretation questions (8 marks), you must choose a specific design discipline — lighting, sound, set, or costume — and commit to it fully. Do not drift between disciplines mid-answer. Name the specific element: a profile lantern with a cobweb gobo, not “spotlights”; a silk dupion jacket in deep crimson with gold epaulettes, not “red costume”; a recorded soundscape of industrial machinery underscored by a low string drone, not “background noise”. For 12-mark intentions questions, go further: explain why the playwright or director would want the audience to feel or understand something at this exact moment, and then show how your design choice delivers that intended effect. Vague descriptors (“dark and moody”, “old-fashioned costume”) are the most common reason students score in the lower bands. Specificity is what separates Mastering from Developing.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four design fundamentals — scale, shape, colour and texture — underpin every design discipline. Every specific design choice can be analysed through one or more of these lenses.
  • Gobos, lighting states, soundscapes, revolves and levels are precision tools. Name them in exam answers. Vague descriptors like “dark lighting” or “period costume” score in the lower bands because they fail to show design thinking.
  • A strong designer answer combines a named element, a specific moment in the play, and a precisely stated effect on the audience’s understanding or emotional response.

practice_questions.text: What is a gobo?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: a metal disc with a cut-out pattern inserted into a profile lantern to project a pattern of light and shadow onto the stage.

practice_questions.text: What is a soundscape in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a soundscape is a layered composition of multiple simultaneous sounds; 1 mark for explaining that it creates an immersive sonic environment that establishes location, atmosphere or mood.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a set designer might use levels to communicate the relationship between two characters to the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for naming levels as a set design tool (e.g. rostra, platform, ramp); 1 mark for explaining how elevated height signals status, power or authority; 1 mark for explaining how a lower-positioned character can appear vulnerable, submissive or trapped; 1 mark for linking the spatial relationship to a specific intended effect on the audience's understanding of the characters' dynamic.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design the lighting for a tense confrontation between two characters at the climax of a play. Refer to specific lighting choices and explain their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two specific lighting choices named with precision (e.g. a tight hard-edged profile lantern above one character in cold blue-white at 80% intensity, cross-fading to a low warm side-light on the other; a slow fade to a near-blackout with a single special on the speaking character's face); each choice is anchored to the climax and linked to a named effect (e.g. 'the contrast isolates each character and prevents the audience from reading the other's reaction, creating suspense'); lantern type, colour and intensity are all specified.

Secure: at least one lighting choice with named elements (lantern type or colour); effect described with some specificity; linked to the moment.

Developing: general lighting ideas (bright on one, dark on other); lantern type or colour not specified; effect on audience generic ('creates tension').

Emerging: basic lighting reference (turn lights down) with no specification; effect not linked to the moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a costume designer might use colour, silhouette and fabric to communicate the themes of power and vulnerability in a production. In your answer, refer to specific costume choices and their intended effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: sustained analysis of how specific costume elements (named colour, fabric texture, silhouette, accessories) communicate the theme of power for one character and vulnerability for another; choices are linked to what the designer intends the audience to understand (e.g. 'the gold brocade coat with padded shoulders signals authority and is read immediately by the audience as a costume of dominance, while the pale, undyed linen with a loose, unstructured silhouette communicates the other character's social fragility'); at least two distinct costume elements analysed with the theme in view throughout.

Secure: clear explanation of how at least two costume choices communicate character or theme; some specific vocabulary (colour, fabric, silhouette) used; theme identified and linked to most choices.

Developing: description of what characters might wear with limited analysis of meaning; theme named but not sustained; specificity low.

Emerging: simple costume descriptions with no thematic analysis; vague colour references without explanation.

practice_questions.text: As a designer working across two disciplines of your choice, explain how you would design a key scene to communicate the playwright's intentions to the audience. Refer to specific choices from each discipline and their combined effect.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: two design disciplines chosen and clearly identified; specific, named choices from each (e.g. a gobo projecting fragmented window-frame shadows in lighting; a worn Victorian wallpaper set with a split cyclorama showing a colourless sky beyond); choices are analysed in terms of the playwright's intended audience effect; the combination of disciplines is discussed (e.g. how the lighting interacts with the texture of the set); the staging logic is internally consistent and the answer is anchored to a specific scene or moment.

Secure: two disciplines identified; mostly specific choices with some named elements; audience effect described; some discussion of how the disciplines work together.

Developing: design ideas from two disciplines but limited specificity; general descriptors used; audience effect implied; no analysis of the interaction between disciplines.

Emerging: general staging description with little or no specification; discipline boundaries blurred; audience effect absent.

Theatrical cosmetics, prosthetics and hair used to alter a performer's appearance in ways visible from the auditorium.

lessons.title: Theatre Spaces: Configuration and Audience
lessons.description: Proscenium, thrust, in-the-round, traverse and promenade: how the space shapes the audience.
lessons.content_html:
The Stage Configuration Question

Before any set is built, any costume is made, or any performer begins rehearsing, a director and designer make a foundational choice: where will the audience sit relative to the performance? This is the performer-audience configuration. It shapes every other decision. A gobo that projects a crisp image in a proscenium theatre becomes irrelevant when the audience sits on three sides. A piece of blocking that puts a performer’s back to the audience is a problem in end-on staging but a routine occurrence in theatre in the round. You need to understand each configuration, its advantages, its limitations, and what it demands of performers and designers.

Key Fact

The six staging configurations are: proscenium arch, thrust stage, theatre in the round, traverse, end-on staging, and promenade. Each creates a different relationship between performer and audience. The configuration a director chooses is itself an interpretive statement about what they want that relationship to feel like.

Proscenium Arch

In a proscenium arch theatre, the arch is a picture frame. The audience sees only one face of the stage. This configuration supports illusionistic staging — elaborate sets, painted backdrops, hidden machinery — because the wings (the offstage areas to either side) are invisible to the audience. Designers can make use of upstage depth to create pictorial compositions, with performers positioned across the width of the stage in what is called a stage picture. The further a performer moves upstage, the smaller and less dominant they appear; moving downstage increases their size, presence and power over the audience’s attention.

The limitation of the proscenium is distance and the fourth wall. The audience is a unified mass of observers watching events they are not part of. Naturalistic theatre often relies on the fourth wall being intact: the characters behave as if they are unaware they are being watched. Brechtian theatre deliberately breaks the fourth wall — a performer steps forward, addresses the audience directly, and destroys the illusion, reminding them they are watching a performance.

Thrust Stage

A thrust stage pushes the performance area out into the auditorium so the audience wraps around three sides. This closes the physical distance between performer and audience and makes proxemics — the use of physical distance as a communicator — more acute: the audience can see the performer’s face and hands with far more detail than in a large proscenium house. A performer standing at the tip of the thrust, surrounded on three sides by the audience, is deeply exposed; there is no upstage safety. Blocking (the pattern of a performer’s movement around the stage) must be designed with all three audience sides in mind. The Elizabethan Globe Theatre used a thrust configuration, and Shakespeare’s plays were written for it.

Theatre in the round places the audience on all four sides. The performance area is typically a central square or circle, entered and exited through aisles between the audience blocks. This creates maximum intimacy — the audience feels they are in the room with the characters, not observing from outside — and maximum exposure for the performer. Every performer’s back is turned to some of the audience at any given moment, which means blocking and movement must keep the action alive and visible from all sides. Designers cannot use tall set pieces that block sightlines, and the lighting rig must light from all directions. In-the-round staging suits plays that explore raw human behaviour and want the audience to feel implicated rather than distanced.

Traverse staging (also called corridor staging) places two audience banks facing each other across a long, narrow performance space. The effect is that both audience groups can see each other across the action, creating a sense of surveillance or voyeurism. Performers travel down the “corridor” and their faces alternate between being visible and hidden to each audience group. This configuration suits plays about conflict, opposition, or social division — the geometry reinforces the idea of two sides watching each other across a contested space.

End-On Staging and Promenade

End-on staging is, in practice, very similar to a proscenium arch arrangement: the audience sits in front, the stage is a rectangle facing them. The difference is that there is no arch frame — the stage and audience share the same continuous space, which can create a slightly less formal, more immediate feel. Many studio or black box theatres are configured end-on because the space is flexible and the seats can be repositioned for a different production.

Promenade staging removes the fixed seating entirely. The audience follows the performers through a series of locations — corridors, rooms, outdoor spaces — or stands in an open space as the action moves around them. The audience becomes part of the physical world of the play. Their proximity is uncontrolled: a performer can address an individual directly, step up close, or move away to the far end of the space, leaving the audience to turn and find the action. Promenade productions require extremely careful stage management because sightlines cannot be guaranteed and the movement of the audience is a variable the director must plan for.

Key Fact

Stage positioning terminology — upstage left, upstage right, upstage centre, downstage left, downstage right, centre stage, stage left and stage right — is always given from the performer’s perspective, not the audience’s. Stage left is to the performer’s left as they face the audience. A performer standing downstage right (close to the audience, on the performer’s right) is at the most dominant position in a traditional proscenium staging, because it is the closest point to the majority of the audience and the eye naturally travels there.

The most common error is to confuse in-the-round (audience on all four sides) with thrust (audience on three sides), or to define a proscenium arch as simply “a normal theatre”. Another error is to forget that end-on is not proscenium — the proscenium arch configuration specifically requires the framing arch. Make sure you can define each configuration precisely, state how many sides of the audience are present, and name one implication for a performer or designer working in that space. The exam can ask you to choose a configuration for a specific dramatic purpose and justify your choice — so know not just what each configuration is, but what it does to the performer-audience relationship.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions about theatre configurations often ask you to “explain the effect” of a particular configuration on the audience or to “analyse the implications” for a designer or performer. A 4-mark answer needs to name the configuration, describe its defining feature (where the audience sits), and explain at least two implications — one for performer and one for designer, or two different effects on the audience relationship. For 8-mark or 20-mark questions where you must choose a configuration, commit to one and justify it: “I would stage this production as theatre in the round because the playwright intends the audience to feel implicated in the events, and the proximity of the in-the-round configuration removes the safety of observation that a proscenium arch provides.” Avoid hedging by describing multiple configurations without committing to one — it reads as uncertainty rather than analysis. Remember: stage left and stage right are always from the performer’s perspective, facing the audience.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The six staging configurations are proscenium arch, thrust, theatre in the round, traverse, end-on, and promenade. Each creates a distinct performer-audience relationship and has specific implications for blocking, sightlines and design.
  • Stage positioning terms (upstage, downstage, stage left, stage right, centre stage) are always from the performer's perspective facing the audience. Downstage is closest to the audience; upstage is furthest away.
  • The fourth wall is the imaginary barrier between the world of the play and the audience. Naturalistic theatre maintains it; Brechtian theatre deliberately breaks it through direct address.

practice_questions.text: In which staging configuration does the audience sit on all four sides of the performance space?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: theatre in the round.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'proxemics' in theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that proxemics refers to physical distance on stage; 1 mark for explaining that it concerns the distances between performers, and between performers and audience, and how those distances communicate power, intimacy or relationship.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a thrust stage affects the performer's use of the performance space compared to a proscenium arch stage.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for correctly defining a thrust stage (performance area extends into the audience, audience on three sides); 1 mark for contrasting with proscenium (audience on one side only, frame separating stage and auditorium); 1 mark for explaining an implication for blocking (the performer must play to three sides; their back is always turned to some of the audience); 1 mark for explaining an implication for audience relationship (greater proximity, more visible physical detail, higher exposure for the performer).

practice_questions.text: Explain how staging a production in the round rather than using a proscenium arch might affect the audience's experience of the performance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for defining theatre in the round (audience surrounds the space on all sides); 1 mark for identifying a specific effect on audience experience (e.g. the audience feels implicated or immersed rather than distanced; they can see each other watching across the space, which emphasises shared community or shared guilt); 1 mark for identifying a limitation or challenge (sightlines cannot be guaranteed; every performer's back is turned to part of the audience); 1 mark for analytical development (e.g. this configuration suits a play that wants the audience to feel unable to escape their role as witness).

practice_questions.text: As a set designer, explain how you would design a set for a traverse stage production. In your answer, discuss how the configuration affects your design choices and what effect your set would have on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: specific understanding of traverse configuration (two audience banks facing each other across a long narrow space); at least two specific set design choices driven by the configuration (e.g. low-profile furniture so sightlines are maintained; a minimal, symbolic central set piece such as a bare table and two chairs to emphasise the confrontational symmetry of the space; floor materials used to define zones rather than walls that would block views); each choice linked to a precise audience effect (e.g. 'the audience on both sides watches the other group watching the performers, which creates a sense that everyone is under surveillance'); scale, shape and texture referenced.

Secure: traverse configuration understood; at least two design choices described with some specificity; audience effect generally described.

Developing: configuration recognised but design choices are generic and not driven by traverse's specific demands; audience effect implied.

Emerging: basic staging ideas with no specific understanding of traverse; little or no discussion of how the configuration shapes the design.

practice_questions.text: As a designer, compare two staging configurations and explain which you would choose for a production exploring themes of surveillance, power and control. Justify your choice with reference to specific design and staging possibilities each configuration offers or denies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: two configurations clearly defined and contrasted; the chosen configuration is justified with reference to the theme (surveillance, power, control) and at least two specific staging/design possibilities it enables (e.g. traverse: the audience watches the action across a contested space, seeing each other watching, which mirrors the theme of mutual observation; in-the-round: the performers are surrounded and cannot escape, embodying the theme of constant scrutiny); specific design choices discussed (set, lighting or sound elements that work with the chosen configuration); the rejected configuration is discussed to strengthen the argument.

Secure: two configurations compared; chosen configuration justified with theme in view; at least one specific staging/design possibility named per configuration; some design vocabulary used.

Developing: two configurations described but comparison is superficial; theme mentioned but not sustained in the argument; design choices general.

Emerging: one or two configurations named with basic description; no clear justification for choice; theme not connected to configuration.

lessons.title: Performer Skills: Voice and Body
lessons.description: Pitch, pace, pause, gesture, posture and proxemics: the full toolkit of performer skills.
lessons.content_html:
Why Performer Skills Matter

A performer communicates character, emotion, and intention entirely through what they do with their voice and body. The audience cannot read the performer’s mind — they can only see and hear what the performer gives them. This means every choice — whether to speak quickly or slowly, whether to stand tall or collapse inward, whether to move toward another character or retreat — must be deliberate, repeatable, and truthful to the character’s situation. The specification separates performer skills into two categories: vocal skills and physical skills. In the exam you will often be asked to write “as a performer” — which means naming specific skills from both categories and anchoring them to a named moment of the play.

Vocal Skills: The Seven Key Elements

The spec identifies nine vocal elements. The seven most frequently tested are: pitch (how high or low the voice sounds), pace (how fast or slow the performer speaks), pause (deliberate silence — one of the most powerful tools in a performer’s kit), volume (how loud or soft), accent (regional or national speech pattern, which communicates class, background and belonging), intonation (the rise and fall of pitch within a phrase, which signals questions, sarcasm, or certainty), and phrasing (how the performer breaks a line into units of meaning, which controls where the emphasis falls and what the audience understands).

Intonation is a subtler skill than volume or pace, but it is the one that determines how a line is understood. The same words can mean entirely different things depending on how they are inflected. A character saying a simple farewell can, through intonation, communicate resignation, contempt, grief, or barely suppressed rage — without changing a single word. Projection is the ability to be heard clearly from the back of the auditorium; it is not simply about being loud, but about placing the voice forward, using breath support and resonance.

Key Fact

A pause is not an accident — it is a deliberate choice. A long pause before answering a question can communicate guilt, calculation, fear, or contempt. A short, clipped pause mid-sentence can signal suppressed emotion. In exam answers, when you name “pause” as a vocal skill, you must explain what the pause communicates at that specific moment — not just that it “creates tension”.

Physical Skills: Voice with the Body

The spec identifies these physical skills: movement, posture, gesture, facial expression, spatial awareness, stillness, timing and control. Posture is perhaps the most immediate physical signal: a character who stands with their shoulders back and chin level reads as confident or authoritative; a character who hunches forward, pulls their shoulders inward, and lowers their gaze reads as cowed, tired, or defeated. Status in theatre is communicated more through posture than through any other single physical tool.

Gesture must be precise and intentional. An aimless wave of the hand is not a gesture — it is a habit. A clenched fist rising slowly to the chest and then stopping tells a very specific story about suppressed emotion. Gesture and speech should either reinforce each other (congruent) or contradict each other (incongruent) — incongruent gesture and speech is a powerful tool for showing a character saying one thing while feeling another. The examiner wants to know not just that you would gesture, but exactly what gesture, at what moment, and to what effect on the audience.

Stillness is the absence of unnecessary movement, used at a moment of intensity so that the audience’s focus sharpens. A performer who has been moving constantly through a scene and then suddenly becomes completely still draws the audience’s eye with great force — the stillness signals that something of significance is happening. Used at a moment of realisation, confrontation, or grief, stillness amplifies emotional impact in ways that movement cannot.

Timing is not just about comedy (though comedy depends on it entirely). Timing is the performer’s ability to land a line, a gesture, or a movement at precisely the right moment relative to what has come before and what will come after. A reaction that arrives a beat too late can read as distracted; a reaction that arrives a beat too early can deflate a moment. Timing requires the performer to listen — to their scene partner, to the sound design, to the rhythm of the scene — and respond within it.

Proxemics: Using the Space

Proxemics — the use of physical distance and spatial relationships on stage — is how a performer communicates the quality of a relationship without words. Characters who are in close proximity signal intimacy, trust, vulnerability, or threat, depending on the context. Characters kept at opposite ends of the stage — one upstage left, one downstage right — communicate distance, estrangement, or reluctance. As a performer, the choice of where to stand relative to another character, and how that distance changes through a scene, is a form of choreography — it maps the emotional journey of the relationship.

The direction of the performer’s body also matters: facing front (full front) is open and available to the audience; in profile (three-quarter turn) suggests the performer is engaged with another character rather than with the audience; back to the audience (full back) is rare in proscenium staging and usually signals a powerful dramatic moment of withdrawal or concealment.

Key Fact

The most common exam error in performer questions is writing “I would say it angrily” or “I would look scared”. These score in the Emerging band because they do not specify a skill. Always translate emotion into craft: “I would lower my pitch and reduce my pace to almost nothing, allowing a three-second pause before the final word, while keeping my body completely still with my gaze lowered to the floor, so the audience sees the character’s grief as something he cannot speak.”

Imagine a scene where a young character finally confronts an older authority figure who has wronged them. As a performer playing the young character, you might begin the speech with a raised pitch and rapid pace — the voice tight and high from adrenaline — then let it slow and drop in pitch as the character finds their authority, ending the speech in a low, measured register with a deliberate pause after the final accusation. Physically, you might start the scene in profile, angled away from the authority figure, then rotate by increments through the speech until you are full-front to both the authority figure and the audience, signalling full confrontation. Your proxemics might move from upstage, close to the exit, toward downstage centre, closing the distance between yourself and the authority figure with each step.

As a lighting designer for that same moment, you might design the opening of the speech in a warm, low-intensity side-light that keeps the young character partially in shadow, signalling their uncertainty. As the character gains courage, you slowly bring up a front-of-house profile lantern in a neutral white, increasing in intensity through the speech, so that by the final accusation the young character is in full, clear, unambiguous light — exposed and resolute. The authority figure, meanwhile, is allowed to drop fractionally in intensity, as though the balance of power is visibly shifting.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For performer interpretation questions (8 marks), you must provide both a vocal AND a physical choice, and both must be specific and anchored to a named moment. “I would say it angrily” has no mark-scheme credit. “I would raise my pitch and quicken my pace for the accusation, then drop to a near-whisper for the final line, while standing in complete stillness with my fists clenched at my sides” names vocal skill (pitch, pace, volume) and physical skill (stillness, gesture) and gives enough detail to be awarded Mastering marks. For 12-mark intentions questions, connect the performer choices to what the playwright intends the audience to understand or feel at that moment — the craft choices are the evidence; the intention is the analysis. For 20-mark extended responses, you must address both performer and designer choices — a 20-mark answer that only discusses performance will be capped at the Developing band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Vocal skills include pitch, pace, pause, volume, accent, intonation, phrasing and projection. Physical skills include posture, gesture, facial expression, movement, stillness, timing and spatial awareness. Both categories must appear in any performer question answer.
  • Translate emotion into craft. Never write “I would say it angrily” — write what the voice does (pitch rises, pace quickens, volume drops) and what the body does (fists clench, back straightens, gaze locks). Specificity earns marks.
  • Proxemics — the physical distance between characters — maps the emotional journey of a relationship. Moving toward another character signals courage, threat or desire; moving away signals fear, withdrawal or rejection.

practice_questions.text: Name one vocal skill a performer might use to communicate a character's nervousness.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of: raised pitch; rapid pace; a stammer or fragmented phrasing; reduced volume (quieter delivery); a prolonged pause before answering; a tremor in the voice.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'projection' as a vocal skill?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that projection is the ability to carry the voice so it is heard clearly by the audience; 1 mark for clarifying that projection is not simply loudness but involves breath support, resonance and forward placement of the voice to reach the back of the auditorium.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer might use stillness and pace to communicate a character's shock at hearing unexpected news.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying stillness as a deliberate physical choice (absence of movement at a moment of intensity); 1 mark for explaining how stillness signals shock to the audience (the sudden stop draws focus and signals something of significance); 1 mark for identifying pace as a vocal choice (slowing to almost nothing, or an abrupt stop); 1 mark for explaining the combined effect on the audience (the audience reads the performer's frozen body and near-silent voice as the outward sign of an inner world that has been overturned).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing a character who is trying to appear confident while concealing fear, explain in detail the vocal and physical choices you would make. Anchor your answer to a specific type of scene or moment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: both vocal and physical choices are named with precise detail; vocal: e.g. a steady, lowered pitch and measured pace to project surface confidence, but a fractional rise in pitch on specific words that betray anxiety, and controlled breathing to prevent a tremor; physical: e.g. upright posture with shoulders deliberately set back, head held at eye level, but fingers interlaced behind the back or a hand pressed lightly against the thigh to manage micro-tremors invisible to the other character but visible to the audience; proxemics: standing in a fixed position rather than moving, because movement might betray instability; choices anchored to a specific moment type (e.g. a job interview, a confrontation with a parent, a public speech).

Secure: both vocal and physical choices present with some specificity; anchored to a moment; effect on audience generally described.

Developing: one category (vocal or physical) described with more detail than the other; limited specificity; effect on audience implied rather than stated.

Emerging: states emotion ('confident but scared') without translating into specific skill choices; no anchoring to a moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a director might use performers' vocal and physical skills to communicate a theme of power and powerlessness in a key scene. Refer to at least two specific skills and their intended effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the theme of power/powerlessness is the sustained lens throughout; at least two specific skills named for each end of the power relationship (e.g. the powerful character: slow, low-pitched deliberate speech; full-front posture with weight planted; minimal gesture; the powerless character: fragmented phrasing, rising pitch; curled posture; retreating proxemics moving away toward the edge of the stage); each choice is analysed for its intended effect on the audience's understanding of the theme (e.g. 'the contrast in posture makes the power differential immediately legible before either character speaks, positioning the audience as witness to a dynamic they recognise'); choices are connected to directorial intention.

Secure: theme identified; at least two skills discussed with some specificity; effect on audience described; directorial intention present.

Developing: relevant skills described but analysis of their thematic function is limited; audience effect implied.

Emerging: skills named without analysis; theme not sustained; audience effect absent.

practice_questions.text: As a performer and a lighting designer working on the same climactic scene, explain how you would use performer skills and lighting design to communicate the scene's emotional turning point to the audience. Refer to specific choices from both disciplines.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a clearly defined emotional turning point; specific, named performer choices (vocal: pitch, pace, pause with precise detail; physical: posture change, proxemics movement, gesture anchored to the turning point); specific, named lighting choices (lighting state, lantern type, colour, intensity, direction — all changing to reflect the turning point); the interaction between performance and lighting is discussed (e.g. 'the performer's physical stillness makes the slow cross-fade in lighting more visible — the change in the world around them mirrors the internal shift'); the combined effect on the audience is precisely stated.

Secure: turning point identified; at least two performer skills and two lighting choices with some specificity; effect on audience described; some discussion of how the disciplines interact.

Developing: one discipline stronger than the other; design or performance choices are general; turning point described rather than analysed; little discussion of discipline interaction.

Emerging: basic performance or design ideas; turning point not clearly defined; audience effect absent; no interaction between disciplines.

glossary_terms.definition: The techniques a performer uses with their voice, including pitch, pace, pause, volume, accent, intonation, phrasing, projection and emotional range.

lessons.title: From Page to Stage: The Rehearsal Process
lessons.description: From read-through to opening night: how directors, performers and designers shape a production.
lessons.content_html:
The Journey from Script to Stage

A script is a set of instructions written by a playwright, but it is not a performance. The gap between the words on the page and a live audience sitting in a darkened theatre is filled by the rehearsal process: weeks or months of collaborative work in which the director, performers, and designers translate the playwright’s intentions into concrete theatrical choices. Understanding the stages of that process — and who is responsible for what at each stage — prepares you to write convincingly about how theatre is made and why it looks and sounds the way it does.

Key Fact

The main stages of a professional rehearsal process are: read-through (the whole company reads the script together for the first time), blocking rehearsals (the director sets the performers’ movement), character and scene work (performers and director develop character depth), production meetings (director and designers align their choices), technical rehearsal (first run in the theatre with all technical elements), dress rehearsal (full run as if performing to an audience), and previews (early performances with a paying audience before opening night).

The Read-Through and Early Rehearsals

The read-through is not a performance — it is a first shared encounter with the text. The director typically introduces the production’s concept at this stage: what world the play will live in, what the central questions are, and what the company is trying to communicate to the audience. Designers may present models and mood boards. Performers begin to form a relationship with their character’s language, but no choices are fixed at this stage.

Early rehearsals are exploratory. The director works scene by scene, often asking performers to try different interpretations: different blocking choices, different emotional approaches, different vocal and physical reads of the same line. This is the phase in which the director discovers whether their concept works in practice, and whether the performers can find genuine truth within it. A director might ask a performer to try playing a scene entirely in stillness, then try it with continuous movement, to find out which communicates more clearly to an audience at the back of the house.

Production Meetings

A production meeting brings the director, designers, stage manager and heads of department together to co-ordinate. At a production meeting the director might clarify that a particular scene requires a lighting special on a specific person from above, or that a costume needs to allow a performer to move extremely quickly. The designer comes back with a solution. Everything discussed is recorded by the stage manager in the production notes, which feed into the prompt copy. Production meetings happen throughout the rehearsal period, not just at the start.

The prompt copy (sometimes called the book) is the most important document in a production. It records every blocking decision, every technical cue — the exact word or action at which the lighting state changes, the sound plays, the flown piece descends — and every note made during rehearsals. During a performance, the stage manager follows the prompt copy and uses it to call cues over the headset system. If the stage manager loses their place, the production is in immediate danger.

Each technical department also produces cue sheets. The lighting operator has a cue sheet listing every lighting state change (LX Q1, LX Q2...) with the moment it occurs and the instruction (fade to black over 3 seconds; snap to lighting state 7). The sound operator has an equivalent document. These cue sheets are prepared by the designer and the stage manager together during and after technical rehearsals.

The Technical Rehearsal

The technical rehearsal (the “tech”) is the first time the production runs with all its elements together: the set, lighting, sound, costumes, props and performers, in the actual theatre. It is notoriously slow. The stage manager calls a cue; the operator runs it; the director watches from the auditorium and gives notes. A single scene of three minutes may take an hour to tech because a lighting state may need refocusing, a sound cue may arrive at the wrong moment, or a scene change may need to be refined. The performers must hit their blocking precisely because the lighting has been focused for specific positions — stand in the wrong place and you will be in darkness or shadow.

Dress Rehearsal and Previews

The dress rehearsal is a full performance run, as close to opening night as possible. Notes are given by the director afterwards but the run is not usually stopped. The purpose is to allow the company to perform the production from first scene to last without intervention, building stamina and confidence. For the stage manager, it is a final check that all cues are in the right place and every transition is smooth.

Previews are early performances with a paying audience, before the production’s official opening night. The audience’s responses in preview — where they laugh, where they are silent, where they seem confused — give the director valuable information. Changes are often made after previews: blocking adjusted, a scene cut, a cue repositioned. Many productions are substantially different on opening night from what they were on the first preview.

Key Fact

The technical rehearsal is the first run with all technical elements in the theatre; it is slow and stop-start, pausing to fix each cue. The dress rehearsal is a continuous run in full performance conditions; it is as close to a real performance as possible. Both come before opening night. Previews (with audiences) come after the dress rehearsal but before opening night.

Questions that ask you to “explain how a director and performers work together” or “describe the stage manager’s contribution to a production” are testing knowledge of the rehearsal process. A common error is to treat theatre as a spontaneous activity — to write as if performers make choices moment by moment in front of an audience. Professional theatre is painstakingly planned. Every lighting cue has been rehearsed. Every piece of blocking has been set. Every sound cue has been placed at a specific moment. The spontaneity the audience experiences is the result of hundreds of rehearsed decisions executed simultaneously. When you write about staging choices in extended-response answers, you are implicitly writing about rehearsal choices: decisions made in advance, tested, refined, and locked in place.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions about the rehearsal process often ask for named stages or the role of a specific person at a specific stage. For 1-mark and 2-mark questions, name the correct stage (read-through, blocking, tech rehearsal, dress rehearsal, preview) and be precise about who is accountable for what. For 4-mark questions, describe a stage, explain what happens at it, and link it to the production’s quality or the audience’s experience. For extended-response (12 or 20 marks) questions that ask you to “direct a production” or “stage a scene”, you are implicitly writing as a rehearsal director — every staging decision you describe is a decision that would have been rehearsed and refined before opening night. Using rehearsal vocabulary (blocking, production meeting, tech, prompt copy) signals to the examiner that you understand how professional theatre actually works, and this raises your answer into the Mastering or Secure band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The rehearsal process moves from read-through (first encounter with the text) through blocking, scene work and production meetings, to the technical rehearsal (first run with all elements), dress rehearsal (full continuous run), and previews (early performances with a paying audience).
  • The stage manager holds the prompt copy — the authoritative record of every blocking and cue decision — and calls all cues during performances. The production meeting co-ordinates all departments and is chaired by the director.
  • Every staging choice in a professional production has been rehearsed, refined and locked. When you write about staging in exam answers, you are writing about rehearsal decisions — using rehearsal vocabulary signals professional understanding.

practice_questions.text: What is the first stage of a professional theatre rehearsal process called?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: read-through.

practice_questions.text: What is blocking in the context of theatre rehearsal?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that blocking is the pattern of movement a performer makes around the stage; 1 mark for explaining that blocking is set by the director during rehearsals and recorded in the prompt copy.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a technical rehearsal and a dress rehearsal, and what each stage contributes to the production.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for accurately describing the technical rehearsal (first run in the theatre with all technical elements, stop-start to fix cues); 1 mark for accurately describing the dress rehearsal (full continuous run in performance conditions, as close to opening night as possible); 1 mark for explaining what the tech contributes (co-ordination of all technical departments, refinement of cue timings); 1 mark for explaining what the dress rehearsal contributes (stamina and confidence for the company; final check that transitions are smooth; a director's last chance for major notes before the audience arrives).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a production meeting contributes to the success of a production, and what the stage manager's role is within it.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for explaining that a production meeting brings director and all design/technical departments together to co-ordinate; 1 mark for giving a specific example of what is discussed or resolved (e.g. the director clarifies where a lighting special must fall; the set designer confirms the delivery date for a piece of scenery; a costume quick-change problem is identified and solved); 1 mark for the stage manager's role (records all decisions in the production notes, which feed into the prompt copy; circulates action points to departments); 1 mark for linking the production meeting to the audience's eventual experience (if departments are not aligned, the production fails technically in front of an audience — production meetings prevent this).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the collaboration between a director and a sound designer during the rehearsal process might shape the audience's experience of a specific scene. In your answer, refer to at least one stage of the rehearsal process and specific sound design choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the collaboration between director and sound designer is analysed through at least one named rehearsal stage (e.g. production meeting where director establishes the emotional intention of a scene; tech rehearsal where the sound cue is placed precisely at the moment a character makes a turning-point decision); specific sound choices named (e.g. a low-frequency drone building under a confrontation scene; a sudden sharp silence on the word of revelation; a diegetic sound cue of distant traffic that is gradually removed to create isolation); the intended effect on the audience is precisely stated and connected to the director's intention.

Secure: collaboration described through at least one rehearsal stage; specific sound choices present; audience effect described; directorial intention generally linked.

Developing: rehearsal process referenced but not used analytically; sound choices are generic; audience effect implied.

Emerging: basic description of sound design with no rehearsal process reference; audience effect absent.

practice_questions.text: As a director, describe the decisions you would make during rehearsals to stage a key scene that involves a sudden reversal of power between two characters. Refer to specific choices from at least two disciplines (performer and one design role) and explain how you would develop these choices through the rehearsal process.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a clearly defined power reversal; specific performer choices developed through named rehearsal stages (e.g. in blocking the powerful character begins downstage centre with the other character upstage; as rehearsals progress the reversal is staged as a physical crossing — the characters swap spatial positions — timed to a specific line); specific design choices from one discipline (e.g. lighting: a cross-fade from a warm state favouring one character to a cold state favouring the other, refined during tech rehearsal); the rehearsal process is used meaningfully (choices are developed and changed during rehearsals, not simply presented as final); the combined effect of performance and design is discussed.

Secure: power reversal identified; performer and design choices present with some specificity; at least one rehearsal stage referenced; audience effect described.

Developing: staging ideas described but limited connection to rehearsal process; design or performance choices are general; audience effect implied.

Emerging: basic staging description with no rehearsal process vocabulary; power reversal not clearly staged; audience effect absent.

glossary_terms.definition: The first stage of the rehearsal process, in which the whole company reads the script aloud together.
The pattern of movement a performer makes around the stage, set by the director during rehearsals and recorded in the prompt copy.
A regular meeting between the director and all design and technical departments to co-ordinate progress and ensure every element of the production is aligned.
The master copy of the script, held by the stage manager, containing all blocking, stage directions, technical cues and creative decisions recorded during the rehearsal process.
Documents listing every technical cue for a department in the order they occur in the performance, with the cue number, trigger and operational instruction.
A rehearsal held in the performance space with the full technical production elements operating for the first time, used to co-ordinate all technical cues with the performers.
A full run of the production in performance conditions, with costumes, make-up, all technical elements and the full cast, as a final preparation before opening to the public.
